newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Cenbank not involved in debt scam - Cardoso.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Cenbank not involved in debt scam - Cardoso.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said the central bank was in no way involved in a multi-million dollar scam involving state and city bonds, local Jornal do Brasil reported on Sunday.
"The Central Bank expressed its disapproval to all requests to issue bonds," Cardoso told the newspaper.

The scandal, billed as potentially one of the biggest to rock Brazilian politics since the downfall of former president Fernando Collor de Mello, centers on claims that brokers and officials may have siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars through suspect municipal and state bond issues.
Several states and some cities are alleged to have sold bonds at well below market prices, ensuring instant profits for brokers and others involved in the scheme.
Cardoso told Jornal do Brasil that the best thing would be to end public bond issues as a source of funding for states and cities.

Under Brazil's constitution, states can only raise money in the market to pay court settlements. Senators said the states in question exaggerated the settlements they had to pay, even falsifying documents and used the excess to cover normal day-to- day expenditures.

Celso Pitta, mayor of Sao Paulo, Brazil's largest city, is expected to be asked to give evidence to a special parliamentary committee which reported receiving documents apparently linking him to the scandal during the time he was the city's finance secretary.
But Pitta has said he has nothing to fear from the investigation and that all operations were legal and profitable.
Besides, he said the Central Bank, whose president at the time was current Finance Minister Pedro Malan, was fully aware of all the city council's financial dealings.
Malan, however, has made public documents in which he expressed his disapproval of the operations while he was head of the Central Bank, newspapers said.

A number of small banks and brokerage houses suspected of being involved in the scandal have already been closed down. But there are now concerns that the investigation may point to some large banks and pension funds.
In his interview with Jornal do Brasil, Cardoso said that the government would not interfere should it emerge that larger institutions were involved.

"With the end of inflation, many things which before passed unnoticed are now coming to the surface. Depending on the course of the investigations.... the results will be highly positive not only for the government but for all society," he said.
